events.article_text:
Japan Poised to Ramp Up LNG Buying as Power Prices Surge

What I Cover My focus spans the global energy landscape and the technologies reshaping it, specifically focusing on oil and gas, renewables, and tech-driven market…

The Federal Reserve will almost certainly raise interest rates on Dec. 9, and it will do it without seeing the November inflation report, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics has scheduled for 8:30 a.m. the next morning. Policymakers are committing to a hike that nearly all of them already expect, and the last report they did see ran hot.

Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% economists expected, and core prices rose 0.3% for the third month in a row. Fed Gov. Christopher Waller has said a quarter-point increase on its own "would put our credibility at risk." The central bank raised rates in September for the first time in three years, then held in October over two dissents from officials who wanted another hike.

What changed is where the heat comes from. Energy prices rose 0.7% in the October index after jumping 5.2% in September, so the pressure now sits in shelter, food and everyday goods, and Waller told CNBC last week that inflation is "spreading out." That takes away the easy argument for energy stocks, which is that crude carries them, and crude doesn't look dependable. It fell again Monday on doubts about AI spending, Iran keeps going after tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump says strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year, and Bank of America and JPMorgan disagree about whether 2027 brings a shortage or a glut.

So the screen for this list was balance sheets first and oil second: companies whose interest bills are small next to their cash flow, and whose profits don't hinge on one barrel price. Five made it, though not all of them pass cleanly.

Exxon's Best Business Right Now Isn't Drilling

Darren Woods, chief executive of ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE: XOM), says the company's third-quarter gains are "lasting improvements, not simply the result of favorable prices and margins." Take that with some salt. Refining earned $9.05 billion of Exxon's $17.5 billion in adjusted profit, more than half, in a quarter when fuel markets were tight. Woods points to $16.9 billion in structural cost savings, and those won't vanish when margins loosen, but a refining windfall can. The Gulf Coast refineries ran at full crude utilization during the quarter and turned out the second-highest diesel volume on record there, so the plants themselves are doing their part.

A rate hike barely matters to a company whose net debt, $22.1 billion at the end of September, is only a little above the $19.1 billion of free cash flow it generated in that single quarter. Exxon still plans $20 billion of buybacks for 2027, assuming markets cooperate.

The soft spots are easy to find if you look for them. Production is down about 2.5% this year, upstream earnings fell on lower prices and the timing of Guyana entitlements, and Exxon booked $921 million of Middle East impacts that it leaves out of adjusted earnings. That is a list that's easier to live with when the refineries are covering for the wells.

Growth projects keep arriving regardless, and Uaru began producing offshore Guyana on Nov. 16, lifting the country's capacity to 1.1 million barrels a day, and a day later Mozambique approved a redesigned Rovuma LNG plan that Exxon expects to sanction by year-end, at a cost Standard Bank puts near $30 billion. A decision that size, announced as the Fed raises rates, will say more about management's confidence than any earnings call.

Texas Pacific Land Collects Rent on Other People's Wells

In the second quarter, Texas Pacific Land Corporation (NYSE: TPL) realized $0.40 per thousand cubic feet of gas. In the third it realized $2.40. TPL had nothing to do with that, because it doesn't drill, and the price of its cut moved anyway. It owns Permian Basin land and gets paid in royalties, water fees and easements when operators work on it, and its third-quarter results set records for revenue, net income and free cash flow.

That structure is why a rate hike hardly registers. Net income was $167.4 million against interest expense of $981,000, and the adjusted EBITDA margin ran about 87%, a figure that looks like a typo until you remember nobody at TPL is paying for a rig. Operators did the work behind the record royalty and water volumes, which is the whole appeal of the model. Water sales revenue slipped on lower prices, and the company's own release warns that revenue depends on commodity prices and on what customers decide to drill.

The more interesting part is what TPL wants to be next. It agreed to supply land and brackish water for Chevron's Project Kilby, a power plant in Reeves County meant to serve a customer's data center, and it finished a 10,000-barrel-per-day desalination plant in Orla.

Chief Executive Tyler Glover says the company is working to turn that groundwork into "meaningful commercial outcomes," wording that stops short of promising revenue. TPL has also spent $122.7 million this year on land in four Texas counties, including sites for data center and power projects.

Valero Made $6.8 Billion and Investors Sold Anyway

Valero Energy Corporation (NYSE: VLO) told investors on Oct. 22 that it had earned $6.8 billion in the quarter, and the shares fell about 4% before the opening bell. The cause was the number behind the profit: a refining margin that tripled to $39.24 a barrel, which the market assumes won't last.

Management says it can, and Chief Operating Officer Gary Simmons pointed out that simple refineries in Asia earn only $2 to $3 a barrel once freight is paid, which keeps a floor under the gap between crude costs and fuel prices, although he also conceded that a jump in crude could squeeze margins. The appeal is that a refiner is a bet on the spread rather than the barrel, so Valero can do fine without oil climbing. Dem

items.title: Japanese bond yields fall as lower oil prices ease inflation concerns
items.summary: Japanese government bond yields declined due to falling oil prices that eased inflation concerns. The 10-year JGB yield reached a two-week low of 2.715%. Meanwhile, Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 index experienced a brief surge of 5% following Nvidia's leadership announcement. Shorter-dated US Treasury yields increased as market stability was reassured by the news. Additionally, markets anticipate a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

analysis.tldr: When foreign borrowing costs shift and big global tech stocks surge, Indian markets react as global investors shuffle their money across countries.
the_story: Japanese government bond yields declined to a two-week low of 2.715% because falling oil prices eased worries about inflation (rising prices of everyday goods).
Japan's main stock market index, the Nikkei 225, jumped 5% briefly after a leadership announcement from the US tech company Nvidia.
Shorter-dated US Treasury yields (interest paid by the US government to borrow money for short periods) increased because market stability was reassured.
Global markets are anticipating a 25-basis-point (a 0.25% change) rate hike by the US Federal Reserve (the US central bank) in December.
analysis.what_happened: Bond yields (the interest rate governments pay to borrow money) in Japan fell because cheaper oil reduced fears of rising inflation. At the same time, global markets reacted to Nvidia's news and traders started preparing for the US central bank to raise interest rates in December.
analysis.analogy: It is like a seesaw in a global playground: when borrowing costs drop in one country or a big tech company makes a splash, money quickly flows back and forth across borders, tilting markets everywhere.
why_it_matters_india: Lower oil prices reduce the import bill for India, which heavily relies on foreign oil.
Expectations of US rate hikes cause global investors to rethink where they keep their cash.
Shifts in global liquidity can trigger foreign investors to pull money out of or pump money into emerging markets like India.
This impacts domestic stock indices and the strength of the rupee against the US dollar.

impacts.rationale: If US rate hike expectations strengthen the dollar, the rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imports costlier for Indians.
Positive global tech sentiment and lower oil prices can lift market mood, which is generally good for local investors.
Positive global tech developments, like those involving Nvidia, often spill over to boost confidence in Indian technology companies.
Falling global oil prices ease domestic inflationary pressures, which can eventually benefit consumers if passed on.

watch_next: The official US Federal Reserve announcement regarding the December interest rate decision
Further movements in global oil prices
analysis.caveats: The article touches on multiple unrelated global markets and trending stocks, so the direct ripple effects on India depend heavily on actual foreign investor capital flows.

items.summary: Rating agency retains India's FY27 growth forecast at 7 per cent but warns that rising inflation and weak farm output could prompt the RBI to raise rates by 25 bps in December

analysis.tldr: If global rating agency S&P's prediction of a domestic rate hike holds true, Indians could face costlier loans and a potential slowdown in economic momentum.
the_story: Credit rating agency S&P lowered India's financial year 2028 (FY28) Gross Domestic Product (GDP [the total value of goods and services produced in a country]) forecast to 7%.
S&P expects an interest rate hike in December.
Only the headline was available for this report, as the full article text was not accessible.
analysis.what_happened: Credit rating agency S&P adjusted its outlook, cutting India's projected economic growth for the 2028 financial year down to 7% while also anticipating that a central bank interest rate hike will happen in December. This outlook suggests S&P foresees conditions like rising inflation [rising prices for everyday goods] or economic overheating that would require borrowing costs to go up.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strict driving instructor telling you to slow down your car (cut the GDP growth forecast) and tapping the brakes (rate hike) because they think you are going too fast.
why_it_matters_india: S&P lowers India's FY28 growth forecast to 7% and expects a December rate hike
A rate hike means banks increase borrowing costs for businesses and individuals
Higher borrowing costs can slow down consumer spending and business investments, leading to a softer economic growth rate
Such global downgrades and tightening expectations can also cause foreign investors to reconsider deploying money in developing markets like India

impacts.target: Bank loan interest rates (home, car, and personal loans)
impacts.rationale: If a rate hike happens in December as expected, banks will raise loan interest rates, making EMIs [equated monthly installments - fixed monthly loan payments] more expensive for ordinary borrowers — generally bad for people with debt.

Slower growth forecasts and expectations of higher interest rates can make stock markets cautious, as businesses face higher costs and potentially lower profits — usually viewed with caution by equity investors.

Weaker growth predictions and tighter monetary policy can sometimes trigger outflows by foreign institutional investors [big foreign investors buying local assets], causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars) — which makes imported goods like crude oil pricier for India.

watch_next: Official statements and inflation data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI [India's central bank that sets monetary policy])
Future reports from S&P and other rating agencies on India's growth path
analysis.caveats: Only the headline was available, so the specific underlying reasons cited by S&P for the forecast cut and rate hike expectation remain unverified.

items.title: Oil prices extend losses, Brent hits near 13-week low while WTI slips below $80

events.article_text:
Japan Poised to Ramp Up LNG Buying as Power Prices Surge

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices remained subdued in early trading on Tuesday, with Brent trading below $90 per barrel despite Iranian claims that three oil tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $88.67 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $79.59 per barrel, both near the lowest in three months, after October highs of over $100 per barrel for both benchmarks.

“Brent has largely lost any upward impetus in recent days as supply conditions remain benign despite the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the market weighs the possibility of a future supply glut against persistent Middle East tensions and shipping disruptions,” Reuters quoted DBS Bank’s head of energy research, Suvro Sarkar, as saying.

“However, risk of prices going up again cannot be ruled out as nothing has moved in US-Iran talks and both parties could move at some point to test the other's resolve in blockading the strait,” Sarkar added.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed three tankers had hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz after they violated the country’s new rules for crossing the waterway. The fact that oil traders dismissed the incidents suggests that reports about oversupply have a stronger effect on trading decisions than tanker traffic disruption in the Persian Gulf.

Even a recent interview of President Trump with Fox News, in which he did not rule out a resumption of hostilities, failed to add fuel to oil prices. “They talk all the time, all they do is talk, but it’s all BS,” President Trump told Fox News correspondents. “They’re more aggressive now than before the election,” the U.S. President said, adding that the Iranian officials are like “professional tap dancers.” He also suggested the U.S. could restart attacks on Iranian targets after the end of the year.

analysis.tldr: Global crude oil prices are sitting near three-month lows because traders care more about an expected oil oversupply than tanker troubles in the Middle East, which keeps import costs contained for India.
the_story: Crude oil prices stayed subdued in early Tuesday trading, with Brent crude at $88.67 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) below $80 at $79.59 per barrel.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed three oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz after breaking new crossing rules.
Oil traders dismissed the tanker mine incidents, focusing instead on expectations of a future supply glut (too much oil) and benign supply conditions.
US President Donald Trump noted in a Fox News interview that he could not rule out a resumption of hostilities with Iran after the end of the year.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices are hovering near three-month lows, dropping down from October highs above $100 per barrel. Even though Iran claimed that three oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz (a vital shipping lane) and US-Iran tensions remain high, oil traders shrugged off the news because they are more worried about a potential global oversupply of oil.
analysis.analogy: It is like a vegetable market where prices are dropping because everyone knows a massive harvest is coming in soon, so people ignore minor delivery delays from one particular truck route.
why_it_matters_india: India imports a vast majority of its crude oil from overseas to meet its energy needs.
When global oil prices stay low or fall, it costs India less foreign exchange to buy that oil.
Cheaper imported oil helps keep domestic fuel and transportation costs in check, lowering inflationary pressures.
A lower oil import bill also supports the rupee (the Indian currency) because the country needs fewer US dollars to pay for oil.

impacts.rationale: Prices are currently near three-month lows as traders focus on oversupply fears rather than Middle East shipping disruptions — good for keeping energy costs low.
Lower global crude oil prices reduce the cost of refining and transporting goods domestically, which is generally good for everyday household expenses.
A cheaper oil import bill means India's central bank needs to spend fewer dollars to buy oil, which helps strengthen or stabilize the local currency.
Sustained lower global crude prices give oil marketing companies room to keep retail fuel prices stable or lower, benefiting everyday consumers.

watch_next: Developments regarding US-Iran talks and potential blockades in the Strait of Hormuz
Official reports on global crude oil inventories and future supply levels
analysis.caveats: The risk of prices spiking remains real if US-Iran tensions flare up into actual military conflict that disrupts shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

events.headline: SFIA India, China’s CCPIT CHEM in pact to promote specialty fertilizers

items.title: SFIA India, China’s CCPIT CHEM in pact to promote specialty fertilizers
items.summary: The partnership aims to strengthen engagement between Indian and Chinese manufacturers, technology providers, exporters and industry stakeholders, opening new avenues for trade, investment, technology transfer and industrial collaboration in specialty fertilizers and agriculture

items.title: SFIA India, China’s CCPIT CHEM in pact to promote specialty fertilizers
items.summary: The partnership aims to strengthen engagement between Indian and Chinese manufacturers, technology providers, exporters and industry stakeholders, opening new avenues for trade, investment, technology transfer and industrial collaboration in specialty fertilizers and agriculture

events.article_text:
The Soluble Fertilizer Industry Association (SFIA), India, and the CCPIT Sub-Council of Chemical Industry, China (CCPIT CHEM), have entered into a partnership to promote bilateral trade, industrial cooperation and business opportunities in the specialty fertilizer and broader agricultural industries.

Under this partnership, CCPIT CHEM, through its Fshow platform, will serve as the official strategic partner of SOMS Specialty Summit in Mainland China, with exclusive responsibility for promoting SOMS and facilitating Chinese exhibitor participation and exhibition space sales.

A media statement said the partnership aims to strengthen engagement between Indian and Chinese manufacturers, technology providers, exporters and industry stakeholders, opening new avenues for trade, investment, technology transfer and industrial collaboration in specialty fertilizers and agriculture.

Promoted by SFIA, SOMS Specialty Fertilizer Summit is an international business platform focused on specialty fertilizers and the wider agricultural ecosystem. Its scope encompasses soluble fertilizers, organic fertilizers, micronutrients, stimulants and biostimulants, agrochemicals, pesticides, insecticides, herbicides, industrial and agricultural chemicals, agricultural machinery, process machinery, packaging, printing, irrigation, software, artificial intelligence, digital agriculture and agricultural consulting.

Through this collaboration, both organisations will undertake reciprocal promotional activities across their respective industry networks, official communication channels, websites, digital platforms and international business networks.

The partnership is expected to facilitate greater Chinese participation in SOMS 2027, while providing Indian companies with opportunities to access Chinese technologies, manufacturing capabilities and international business networks.

Quoting Rajib Chakraborty, President of SFIA, the statement said: “Specialty fertilizers are becoming increasingly important to the future of Indian agriculture, particularly in improving nutrient use efficiency, crop productivity and sustainable farming practices. India and China have significant opportunities to complement each other’s strengths in manufacturing, technology and agricultural innovation. This strategic partnership is intended to go beyond exhibitions and create a sustainable platform for industry-to-industry cooperation, technology exchange and business development in specialty fertilizers and the broader agricultural sector.”

events.headline: At Ujani Dam, villagers draw a line against AI data centre and solar projects

items.title: At Ujani Dam, villagers draw a line against AI data centre and solar projects
items.summary: In Solapur district, farmers and fisherfolk say the projects were finalised without consulting them and threaten land, water, and livelihoods already strained by drought and pollution.

events.article_text:
Published : Nov 23, 2026 17:51 IST - 16 MINS READ

A view of the Ujani Dam from the adjacent Jalpari Park near Bhimanagar, on November 13. | Photo Credit: Gautam Nirmal Doshi

“Whoever is against the construction of the AI data centre, please raise your hands,” came an announcement around 11:30 am on November 13 during a Gram Sabha held in Ranzani village in Maharashtra’s Solapur district, by the banks of the Bhima river. Every villager present, young and old, including onlooking children, raised their hands in unison. “The AI data centre and all remaining projects should be cancelled,” said many.

Villagers from Ranzani, the neighbouring Hingangaon village on the other side of Bhima, and the Bhimanagar area that surrounds the Ujani Dam, which holds the 337 square kilometre Ujani Reservoir, are all opposing the proposed construction of not only a 1.4 gigawatt (GW) hyperscale data centre but also a 2 GW floating solar power project and a 1.8 GW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The plans for all these were finalised without consulting farmers, fishermen, and other residents.

The projects are a scaled-down version of initial plans that included a green hydrogen plant and a small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear project. After public backlash and citing feasibility concerns, District Collector S. Karthikeyan announced the cancellation of two of the five projects on November 4. The projects are public-private partnerships (PPP) between the State government’s Water Resources Department, JW Global, and The SEED Consortium Partners, with an initial projected investment of Rs.1.65 lakh crore. The 1.4 GW hyperscale data centre represents almost 70 per cent of this investment.

The projects are envisioned under the banner of making the area a “Sustainable Eco-Enterprise District” or SEED, using 568.15 hectares of land on either side of the Bhima river. It envisages the creation of 40,000 temporary jobs and 2,800 permanent jobs. With almost all local farmers and fishermen unequivocally against the project, fearing its harmful effects on the environment, the question that arises is: who is the development for?

With the mask of decarbonisation initiatives amid rising power and water-centric burdens of data centres adding to the other concerns around data centres, it begs the question why such projects are being implemented in agricultural and fishing areas where livelihoods of entire villages are at stake.

In Maharashtra, this is the second uproar against a data centre, the first being at Thane, where residents are opposing the upcoming 400-plus MW data centre in Balkum.

Speaking at a press conference on November 4, Karthikeyan announced that “not a single guntha of land of farmers will be acquired for the project”. He added: “There will be no compulsory land acquisition. Whatever land is with Maharashtra’s irrigation department, only that will be used. It will be given to the MIDC, which will then tie up with the private company.”

On the concern that some of the land proposed for the projects was farming land, Karthikeyan said: “We’re not going to evict or destroy farms and start the project. We will work out a fair compensation with the farmers.” He said that over 112 hectares (of the 586 hectares required for the project) are currently used by around 70 farmers.

Speaking to Frontline, farmers spoke of how their parents or grandparents had given up land some 50 years ago for the construction of the Ujani Dam. “My family gave up several acres for the Ujani Dam. A lot of that land is unutilised, so as per the law, shouldn’t we get it back?” said Vishwas Shahurao Deokar, a farmer from Hingangaon.

In the presence of authorities and the police, at a Gram Sabha on November 13, Ranzani villagers unanimously opposed the construction of the proposed data centre and two other projects fearing adverse effects on the environment and the livelihoods of farmers and fishermen. | Photo Credit: Gautam Nirmal Doshi

Deokar was referring to Section 101 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (or the LAPR Act, 2013), which states that “when any land acquired under this Act remains unutilised for a period of five years from the date of taking possession, the same shall be returned to the original owner or owners or their legal heirs, as the case may be, or to the land bank of the appropriate government by reversion in the manner as may be prescribed by the appropriate government”.

The land was acquired for building a dam, which is considered a public purpose. But the data centre, with the BESS and floating solar panels serving the data centre, are private ventures.

Colin Gonsalves, a senior advocate at the Supreme Court, said: “The data centre is not a public purpose. When the government acquires land for a public purpose, it must be utilised accordingly. The land vests with the government, so if they don’t use it for a dam and say they want to use it for another public purpose, like a public hospital, that would be permissible. But this data centre is not a public purpose.”

However, if the matter is escalated to the courts, there is a chance that it can be argued that the data centres are being used for a public purpose, Gonsalves added. This is because, in the Union Budget 2022-23, the government included data centres in the “Harmonised List of Infrastructure”, which treats them like national highways, airports, and power grids that have public purposes.

Also Read | A data centre mired in controversy

Even though there is no direct utilitarian benefit for farmers or fishermen, the data centres set up by private companies could be deemed to hold a public purpose, if questioned.

The farmers from Hingangaon said that they just want their land back. They wanted to know why the project could not come up on barren land and why it had to be near the Ujani Dam area. “We grow sugar cane, bananas, pomegranates, wheat, and more here. This

analysis.tldr: Local protests over a massive data centre and green energy project in Maharashtra could delay large private infrastructure investments in the region.
the_story: Villagers in Ranzani, Hingangaon, and around Maharashtra's Ujani Dam unanimously opposed a proposed 1.4 gigawatt AI data centre, a floating solar project, and a battery storage system during a November 13 Gram Sabha.

The projects are part of a public-private partnership between the Maharashtra Water Resources Department, JW Global, and The SEED Consortium Partners, with an initial investment of Rs 1.65 lakh crore.

District Collector S. Karthikeyan previously cancelled two of the five initial projects (a green hydrogen plant and a nuclear project) on November 4 following public backlash, promising no compulsory land acquisition for farmers.

Farmers argue that some of the land was originally given up for the Ujani Dam 50 years ago and should be returned under Section 101 of the Land Acquisition Act, 2013, since it is now being used for private commercial ventures.

Legal experts note that while the data centre is a private venture, it might be legally defended as serving a public purpose because the Union Budget 2022-23 included data centres in the Harmonised List of Infrastructure.
analysis.what_happened: Villagers in Maharashtra's Solapur district strongly rejected a massive Rs 1.65 lakh crore technology and clean energy project backed by the state government and private companies. The backlash happened because locals were not consulted about projects affecting their farming and fishing lands near the Ujani Reservoir, forcing the district administration to scale back initial plans.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family being asked to give up part of their backyard for a giant corporate warehouse without being consulted, only to find out it threatens their daily livelihood.
why_it_matters_india: Protests halt local land use -> infrastructure and technology projects face heavy delays
Delays in large investments -> potential slowdown in regional commercial tech expansion in Maharashtra
National policy classification (Harmonised List of Infrastructure) -> courts may have to decide if private tech hubs count as public utilities
Broader rural pushback -> other states and companies may rethink how they select land for large technology hubs

impacts.target: Infrastructure and real estate investments in Maharashtra
impacts.rationale: Local resistance and legal disputes over land can delay mega projects, slowing down short-term capital deployment in the state.

watch_next: Whether the affected farmers escalate the land dispute to the courts
Further statements or relocations of data centre plans by the Maharashtra government and corporate partners
analysis.caveats: The article cuts off before detailing the final response of the private developers or whether the project will be entirely relocated.

events.headline: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

items.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.summary: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models…

events.article_text:
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.” “If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

analysis.tldr: New scientific warnings about a popular climate-fighting technique could limit its use, potentially affecting plans that previously showed big agricultural boosts for small farmers in India.
the_story: Tech companies like Google and Microsoft have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to startups practicing enhanced rock weathering (ERW), which involves spreading crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms to trap carbon.
Influential models previously estimated that ERW could remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year and potentially boost crop yields by improving soil quality.

A pair of new preprint studies led by the nonprofit CarbonPlan warn that adding too much rock can push soil pH past neutral into alkaline territory, causing micronutrient deficiencies and potentially reducing crop yields.
Limiting rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink ERW's carbon removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year.
A Yale researcher noted that a recent study found ERW boosted median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%, highlighting the stakes for subsistence farming.
analysis.what_happened: Researchers at CarbonPlan released preprint studies showing a hidden trade-off in enhanced rock weathering. While spreading crushed rocks on farms traps carbon dioxide and can initially help soil, adding too much over time makes the soil too alkaline, which can harm crops and reduce harvests.
analysis.analogy: It is like adding fertilizer to help plants grow: a little helps, but dumping too much will eventually burn and kill the crops.
why_it_matters_india: Tech startups and climate models previously projected that rock weathering could significantly boost yields for smallholder farmers in India (by over 20% in one recent study).
The new findings reveal that adding too much rock over time harms soil health and crops rather than helping them.
To protect their harvests, farmers may have to heavily cut back on how much rock they use.
This reduces the overall amount of carbon dioxide that can be removed globally, dampening the expected agricultural benefits for developing regions like India.

impacts.target: Fertilizer & agricultural input demand in India
impacts.rationale: If rock weathering methods must be restricted to protect crops, farmers might rely more on traditional chemical fertilizers and soil treatments.

watch_next: Final peer-reviewed publication of the CarbonPlan studies
Real-world trials of rock weathering on farms in India and globally
analysis.caveats: The new studies are preprints that have not yet been fully peer-reviewed by other scientists.

events.headline: Marape reassures Beijing after PNG’s pacts with the West

items.title: Marape reassures Beijing after PNG’s pacts with the West
items.summary: Infrastructure, roads and gas money explain why Port Moresby will play both sides in the China–US rivalry.

events.article_text:
China's President Xi Jinping shakes hands with Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape before leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) on 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China (Getty Images)

Infrastructure, roads and gas money explain why Port Moresby will play both sides in the China–US rivalry.

Marape reassures Beijing after PNG’s pacts with the West

PNG Prime Minister James Marape spoke to (Opens in new window) Xi Jinping in Shenzhen ahead of the APEC Summit last week, telling China’s President that the decision to close Taiwan’s representative office in Port Moresby had been politically difficult and expressed “hope ​this assists you in your efforts for reunification”.

Marape’s remarks stand out for two reasons. First, Marape appears to have gone further than previous PNG prime ministers by explicitly supporting reunification. Second, his statement may reflect an effort to reassure Beijing following PNG’s recent security agreements with Australia and the United States.

More broadly, the episode illustrates the difficulties PNG faces in maintaining an independent foreign policy while engaging with competing powers.

PNG recognised Beijing in 1976, apart from a brief switch to Taiwan in 1999 – but recognising Beijing’s government is different from explicitly backing reunification. Successive PNG governments have generally avoided taking direct positions on how the dispute should be resolved. Marape may be the first PNG prime minister to publicly endorse reunification in such direct terms.

For Canberra and Washington, the lesson is that security agreements do not guarantee broader foreign policy alignment.

One possible explanation is PNG’s growing economic relationship with China (Opens in new window), including infrastructure financing, market access, investment and development assistance. In this meeting, Marape urged Chinese companies to invest in downstream processing (Opens in new window).

But closing Taiwan’s office also carries economic costs. Taiwan announced that it would stop purchasing PNG’s liquefied natural gas (LNG). Last year, Taiwan had imported 1.8 million tonnes (Opens in new window) of PNG LNG worth about (Opens in new window) $800 million.

For Beijing, Taiwan is a core political issue, giving Marape’s statement considerable diplomatic weight. Xi acknowledged PNG’s position, praising Marape for having “firmly adhered to the ‘one China’ principle”.

Marape’s admission that closing Taiwan’s office was politically difficult was equally interesting. He told Xi: “I faced challenges from within, because we also relate to many nations, but we were resolved.” Public opinion was probably not the main obstacle: foreign policy rarely features (Opens in new window) in PNG’s domestic debates, which are dominated by employment, inflation, public services and law and order, while China and Taiwan remain the preserve of a small urban, political and academic elite.

Marape may instead have been referring to resistance within government, the bureaucracy or PNG’s security establishment – or indirectly acknowledging concerns from the United States. The US State Department described Taiwan’s office closure as “yet another example of Beijing’s intimidation campaign against Taiwan”. Although there is no direct evidence Canberra opposed the move, Marape would have been aware of its concerns. His reference to PNG’s relationships with “many nations” may have been deliberately ambiguous, allowing him to demonstrate political commitment to Beijing without identifying those who may have opposed the decision.

Marape’s remarks may also be read against PNG’s expanding security ties (Opens in new window) with Australia and the United States – the 2023 Defence Cooperation Agreement with Washington and the 2025 Pukpuk Treaty with Canberra – which may have left Beijing fearing PNG was drifting into the Western security architecture.

Marape’s explicit support for reunification challenges that perception, reassuring Beijing that PNG remains committed to the bilateral relationship despite its growing security cooperation with Western partners, and that defence agreements do not determine its diplomatic positions on other issues. Marape reinforced this message by invoking sovereignty:

“China respects the sovereignty of Papua New Guinea. We must give full respect for the sovereignty of China.”

Although directed at Beijing, he may have had a secondary audience. If Australia and the United States assume PNG is already firmly within their sphere of influence, they may have less incentive to compete for its cooperation. Maintaining constructive relations with Beijing gives PNG additional diplomatic and economic options.

China remains an economic partner PNG cannot easily abandon – and neither Australia’s development aid (Opens in new window) nor the United States’ expanded security role gives either country real leverage to change that.

China provides infrastructure financing, investment, construction services and access to markets. In fact, Chinese state-owned enterprises dominate (Opens in new window) the infrastructure sector, implementing projects financed by multilateral institutions, including the Asian Development Bank. Chinese economic involvement consequently extends beyond projects directly financed by Beijing.

Roads, bridges and other visible projects are especially important in PNG politics, to allow politicians to demonstrate that they are delivering to their constituencies. The Connect PNG (Opens in new window)road program is illustrative of the relationship between infrastructure development and political popularity. This road network is intended to connect 13 economic corridors and provinces not previously linked by roads. Marape this year led a convoy of 100 vehicles (Opens in new window) over 830 kilometres from Port Moresby to Morobe Province – on what is now named Pangu Highway, after his own party, and built largely by Chinese contra

events.headline: EU launches safeguard investigation into certain composite input materials

items.title: EU launches safeguard investigation into certain composite input materials
items.summary: On 23 November 2026, the European Union notified the WTO’s Committee on Safeguards that it had initiated, on the same day (23 November 2026), a safeguard investigation into imports of certain composite input materials.

events.article_text:
In the notification, the EU indicated, among other things, as follows:

"4. Provide a point of contact for the investigation and identify the preferred means for corresponding.

Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security

5. Deadlines and procedures to present evidence and views by interested parties

In order to obtain the information it deems necessary for its investigation, the Commission has published questionnaires, available at the website of the Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security(1). The completed questionnaires must reach the Commission within 21 days from the date of initiation.

All interested parties are invited to make known their views in writing, submit information and to provide supporting evidence. Representations in a free format should be submitted within 21 days from the date of initiation. Interested parties may make themselves known by contacting the Commission, preferably by e-mail, immediately but no later than 15 days after the date of initiation. Any submission of views and information after the above deadlines may be disregarded.

All interested parties may also apply to be heard by the Commission within 21 days of the day of initiation. All written submissions in the investigation should be filed with the Commission as set out in the Notice of Initiation."

The notification is available in G/SG/N/6/EU/6.

A safeguard investigation seeks to determine whether increased imports of a product are causing, or are threatening to cause, serious injury to a domestic industry.

During a safeguard investigation, importers, exporters and other interested parties may present evidence and views and respond to the presentations of other parties.

A WTO member may take a safeguard action (i.e. restrict imports of a product temporarily) only if the increased imports of the product are found to be causing, or threatening to cause, serious injury.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: If Indian companies sell these specific input materials to Europe, they might face temporary trade hurdles or extra taxes if Europe decides imports are harming its local factories.
the_story: The European Union (EU) has officially launched a safeguard investigation into certain composite input materials, according to a WTO (World Trade Organization) notification.
The investigation is being handled by the Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security, which has published questionnaires for interested parties.
Interested parties—such as importers and exporters—have 15 days to contact the Commission and 21 days to submit completed questionnaires, evidence, and written views.
A safeguard investigation aims to check if rising imports are causing or threatening serious injury to a domestic industry, which can legally allow the EU to temporarily restrict those imports.
analysis.what_happened: The European Union started a formal investigation into certain composite input materials to see if a surge in imports is hurting its own local industries. Because of WTO rules, the EU must investigate and find proof of serious harm before it can legally put temporary limits on these foreign products.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local shopkeeper complaining to the market association that a new cheap supplier is destroying his business, so the association steps in to look at the sales records before deciding whether to ban or tax the new supplier.
why_it_matters_india: The EU is investigating composite input materials, which can include manufactured goods and raw materials exported by various global players, including India.
If Indian exporters of these materials are caught in the investigation, they must fill out questionnaires and provide evidence within 21 days.
If the EU finds that imports are harming local European businesses, it may place temporary restrictions or import duties.
Higher trade barriers could slow down exports from Indian manufacturing and chemical sectors to Europe, impacting company revenues.

impacts.target: Export revenues of Indian companies selling composite materials to Europe
impacts.rationale: If the EU eventually slaps restrictions on these materials, Indian exporters might sell less—which is bad for those companies' earnings.
This specific investigation is narrow, but broader global trade friction can make overall stock markets slightly nervous.

watch_next: Whether Indian industry groups or specific exporters submit evidence to the European Commission within the 21-day deadline
Any final decision by the EU on whether to impose temporary import restrictions
analysis.caveats: The provided text only gives the procedural rules for the investigation and does not name specific countries or companies targeted, so the exact impact on India depends on whether Indian firms are major exporters of these materials.

history.title: India pledged its gold and changed course
history.what: With foreign reserves down to about two weeks of imports, India physically flew 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England as collateral for an emergency loan. Within weeks the government devalued the rupee twice and began dismantling the licensing system that had governed Indian industry since independence.
history.why: Decades of import substitution had produced an economy that could not earn enough foreign exchange. The Gulf war spiked oil prices and cut remittances from Indians working in the Gulf simultaneously. The Soviet Union, a major trading partner, was collapsing. Political instability meant credit lines were pulled. Several slow problems arrived together with one fast shock — the usual anatomy of a crisis.
history.impact: The rupee fell about 20% in two days. Inflation hit 13%. But what followed was the most consequential economic change in modern Indian history: industrial licensing was abolished, import tariffs that reached 300% began falling, and foreign investment was allowed in.
history.policy: Liberalisation — of licensing, trade and investment — plus a managed floating rupee instead of a fixed one, and a deliberate policy of accumulating foreign exchange reserves so it could never happen again.
history.consequence: India's growth rate roughly doubled over the following two decades. The companies that dominate the Nifty today — the private banks, the IT exporters, the consumer giants — are largely creatures of the post-1991 settlement. And the reserve-hoarding instinct stuck: India now holds well over a year of import cover, which is why rupee wobbles since have been uncomfortable rather than existential.
history.pattern: Crises are when structural reform becomes politically possible. Changes that were unthinkable for forty years were passed in weeks because the alternative was default. The investment lesson is the flip side: the point of maximum fear is often the start of the best decade.
history.india_echo: This is the founding event of the market you invest in. Every time you read that foreign investors are selling, remember that they were only allowed to buy at all because of a fortnight in 1991 when the country nearly ran out of dollars.
history.watch_for: Import cover measured in months of reserves. It is the single number that separates a currency having a bad week from a country having a crisis.
